title: model-arch-performance-notes-llama-mistral-qwen-moe-long-context-analysis
content:
Purpose:
Quick notes from recent profiling and benchmarks comparing Llama-family, Mistral, and Qwen-style model variants across long-context regimes and MoE routing cases. Goal is to highlight architecture-specific bottlenecks we observed on A100/H100 and give actionable mitigations for the serving runtime (kernel selection, KV/cache strategy, batching, and routing heuristics).

Environment & methodology:
- Hardware: experiments run on A100 80GB (persistence mode on) and H100 (where noted).
- OS/stack: Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 11.8/12.1 depending on node, cuBLAS/cuBLASLt, cuDNN, Triton kernels (custom runtime), and our in-house fast-attention/fused-kernel set.
- Profiling: Nsight Systems (+ timeline), CUPTI traces for kernel breakdown, Linux perf for CPU-side hotspots, and flamegraphs for host threads.
- Workloads: sequence lengths = [2048, 8192, 32768], batch sizes = [1, 2, 8], generation step measured as time per token (end-to-end including host prep and post-processing).
- Quantization: evals included FP16 baseline and 8-bit/4-bit quantized variants via our quantization pipeline.
- MoE: evaluated a 32-expert MoE layer proto (sparse routing) with gating + top-k expert selection; routing simulated both CPU-side batching and fused GPU routing kernels.

High-level findings (summary):
- Llama-family (dense) is predictable: attention compute and KV cache memory bandwidth dominate for long-context. With well-optimized attention (flash attention variants) latency scales mostly with sequence length and KV cache reads/writes.
- Mistral variants show better memory locality in our kernels (smaller MLP weight footprint and effective memory access pattern), resulting in 10-20% lower per-token latency at mid-range sequences (2048-8192) on A100 vs Llama with same param count.
- Qwen-style models (larger context optimizations / slightly different positional handling) show higher single-token latency at small batch sizes due to overheads in rotary/positional embedding handling and some extra host-side preprocessing; throughputs improve with batching.
- MoE routing introduces two classes of bottlenecks: routing (gating + top-k selection) and expert dispatch (scatter/gather memory traffic). Naive CPU routing + GPU expert compute is heavily latency-sensitive for interactive use; fused GPU routing reduces overhead but requires careful memory layout.

Detailed observations by architecture:
1) Llama (dense)
- Bottlenecks: KV cache memory bandwidth and attention kernel latency. For seq=32768 we saw >60% of end-to-end time spent in KV read/write (memcpy-like patterns) and attention kernels.
- Profiling notes: Nsight timelines show long contiguous GPU memcpy windows aligned with KV refresh. cuBLAS matmul was not the dominant time sink when flash-attention was enabled; attention kernels accounted for >50% of kernel time otherwise.
- Mitigations: enable prefix-KV caching (avoid redundant device->host sync), use sharded KV layout to improve coalesced reads, and ensure flash-attention fused kernels are used for QKV->attn path. Also earlier eviction heuristics for old KV shards reduce working set on very long contexts.
- Numbers (A100, batch=1): seq=2048 ~ 35-45 ms/token, seq=8192 ~ 70-90 ms/token, seq=32768 ~ 240-320 ms/token (high variance depending on KV layout). Quantized 8-bit brought ~1.6x speedup but memory bandwidth remained limiting for longest sequences.

2) Mistral (dense but different MLP shaping)
- Bottlenecks: MLP projection and weight-load patterns; attention still significant but less dominant than Llama at mid-context lengths.
- Profiling notes: smaller, more contiguous MLP weight blocks improved cache utilization for GEMMs; our Triton kernels for MLP fused with activation improved throughput. CPU-side overhead lower than Qwen.
- Mitigations: favor fused MLP kernels, reduce kernel launch overhead by batching small matmuls, exploit grouped GEMM paths when possible.
- Numbers (A100, batch=1): seq=2048 ~ 28-38 ms/token (10-20% faster than Llama baseline), seq=8192 ~ 60-75 ms/token. For very long contexts (>16k) advantage shrinks because KV dominates.

3) Qwen family (positional handling, tokenization differences)
- Bottlenecks: positional/preprocessing overhead, certain fused ops not available in upstream libs, host-side tokenization and precompute for complex positional embeddings.
- Profiling notes: host threads doing positional embedding offsets and attention mask prep showed non-trivial CPU time (5-15% of end-to-end for small batches). On GPU, lack of a highly-optimized custom attention kernel for some Qwen variants meant we fell back to a slower path.
- Mitigations: move positional offset precompute to GPU (one-time per request where possible), implement fused kernels for the model-specific attention path, and add an input-level micro-batching window to amortize host overhead.
- Numbers (A100, batch=1): seq=2048 ~ 40-55 ms/token; with small micro-batch (b=2) improves ~10-25% depending on sequence length.

4) MoE (sparse experts, routing)
- Bottlenecks: gating / top-k selection (CPU or GPU), scatter/gather for expert dispatch (memory amplification), load imbalance across experts, and extra device synchronization.
- Observations:
  - CPU routing + host->device dispatch added 30-120 ms per token for interactive (depending on batch).
  - GPU-fused routing kernel reduced overhead to ~8-20 ms per token, but required expert weights laid out contiguously per-expert and preallocated scratch buffers to avoid fragmentation.
  - Imbalanced routing (hot experts) caused tail latency spikes; dynamic re-sharding helped but increases complexity.
- Mitigations: implement fused top-k GPU kernel, use per-expert contiguous storage, maintain runtime expert-load statistics and fallback to deterministic round-robin or replica-stride mapping when imbalance exceeds threshold, and add an admission controller to cap tokens routed to sparse layers for strict latency SLOs.
- Numbers (A100, MoE 32 experts, batch=1): naive routing seq=2048 -> +80-150 ms/token overhead vs dense baseline; fused routing -> +10-30 ms/token. With larger batches, MoE becomes more throughput-efficient but remains worse for strict single-request latency SLOs unless routing is highly optimized.

Cross-cutting bottlenecks & runtime recommendations:
- KV/cache layout: For long-context workloads, memory bandwidth and allocation patterns are the top constraint. Use a streaming KV layout (chunked per-layer per-token) to improve coalescing, and avoid per-token device->host synchronization.
- Kernel selection: prefer flash-attention/causal-attn fused kernels for seq > 2k; fallback to cuBLAS paths only when fused kernels not supported. Maintain kernel registry per-model-variant so runtime picks best path automatically.
- Host overhead: tokenization, positional precompute, and routing decisions are cheap per-token but add up. Move as much prep to GPU and amortize with micro-batching for interactive workloads.
- Quantization: 8-bit gives good speedups but may change memory access patterns; test quantized kernels for attention/KV paths specifically. 4-bit requires different kernel codepaths and can worsen memory-coalescing if blocks are not aligned.
- Batching & admission control: for interactive RL/assistant flows, auto-microbatching (short time-window) balances latency vs throughput. For MoE, cap per-request tokens hitting sparse layers to maintain tail latency SLOs.

Open questions & next experiments:
- Evaluate H100-specific kernels (TensorRT fused ops) for Qwen variants - hypothesize 15-30% reduction in host overhead and kernel time.
- MoE: prototype more advanced routing (approximate top-k on-device) to reduce gate CPU time; measure accuracy/perf tradeoffs.
- Long-context KV eviction policies: run controlled experiments on different chunk sizes (256/512/1024 tokens) to find sweet-spot for bandwidth vs extra kernel overhead.
- Investigate hybrid MLP/attention fusion for Mistral to push more compute into contiguous GEMM-friendly paths.

Quick-action checklist (engineer-friendly):
- [ ] Add model-variant kernel registry entries for Qwen attention path (assign TODO to runtime team).
- [ ] Implement fused GPU gating kernel prototype for MoE (assign to sr-engineering / applied-ml).
- [ ] Add KV layout option: "chunked-per-layer" with contiguous device allocation (runtime config flag + perf test).
- [ ] Add micro-batching window config to hosted API to amortize host prep for Qwen and small-batch users.
- [ ] Benchmark H100/TensorRT path for Qwen + Mistral (follow-up perf sweep ticket JIRA-INF-2145).

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Might be worth a small infra-side evaluator that runs live tail-latency tests with MoE enabled vs disabled on canary capacity to measure real traffic impact.
- Add debug traces for expert-utilization over time (small sidecar metric) to help decide when to re-shard.

End of notes.
